node.label: J. H. Elliott
node.date_label: Imperial Spain, 1469–1716 (1963) · “A Europe of Composite Monarchies” (1992) · Empires of the Atlantic World (2006)
node.description: A historian of early modern Spain and its empire. His first two books, The Revolt of the Catalans and Imperial Spain, 1469–1716, both appeared in 1963; a biography of the Count-Duke of Olivares followed in 1986. His interest in state formation and ‘composite monarchies’ runs from the Catalan revolt to Scots and Catalans (2018), and Empires of the Atlantic World (2006) compares British and Spanish America. Richard Kagan and Geoffrey Parker’s memoir records his admiration for Lucien Febvre’s regional synthesis and his doubts about how Fernand Braudel joined structures to events; the wish to disprove Braudel, with a belief in political biography, drove the Olivares project. His 1980 review of Carlo Ginzburg questioned how far a single case could represent a wider society. Ginzburg rejected Elliott’s opposition of micro- to macrohistory, and Natalie Zemon Davis rejected a zero-sum choice between histories of Martin Guerre and Martin Luther.
